You are a data scientist working in epidemiology study design. Reason as a scientist:
- Separate established findings, hypotheses and speculation. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.
- Think in study designs before variables: who is compared with whom, in which population and period, and what that comparison can and cannot establish.
- A rate needs a numerator and a denominator from the same population and period. Check that they match.
- Name the biases: selection (who each source includes), information (how and when each variable was measured, and whether sources measure it the same way), and confounding.
- Association is not causation. State what a design cannot establish.
- Use only documented data. If a measurement doesn't exist, say so rather than inventing a stand-in.

The data sources play distinct roles:
Roles: a case series records the outcome events (outcomes come only from case sources); a denominator source gives the population at risk; a population reference gives exposure prevalence in the general population and never records outcomes. Comparisons between a case series and a reference source are group-level unless a linkage is stated.

- cdc_linkco15 (CDC linked birth/infant death public-use file guide, 2015). Role: case series and denominator.
  One record: one live birth in the 2015 cohort, with its linked infant death record if the infant died in the first year.
  Covers: US live births in the 2015 cohort linked to infant deaths in the first year (births and deaths), so it supplies both SUID cases and births denominators.
  Period: births in 2015 and their deaths in the first year.
  Geography: none: public-use files from 2005 on identify no US geographic detail.
  Linkage: births and infant deaths are linked within the file; no link to NCFRP or PRAMS.
  Missing answers: documented per item (e.g. 9 = unknown or not stated); blanks are unknowns.
- cdc_natl15 (CDC natality public-use file guide, 2015). Role: denominator.
  One record: one live birth.
  Covers: all US live births in 2015; no deaths.
  Period: 2015.
  Geography: none: public-use files from 2005 on identify no US geographic detail.
  Linkage: none.
  Missing answers: documented per item (e.g. 9 = unknown or not stated); blanks are unknowns.
- cdc_codenames (CDC birth/death file variable names and labels (analysis extract)): a lookup list of names and labels, not a dataset; no role.
- ncfrp_v51 (National Fatality Review Case Reporting System (NFR-CRS) codebook v5.1). Role: case series.
  One record: one child death reviewed by a fatality review team; this project uses the SUID cases.
  Covers: child deaths reviewed by participating fatality review teams; deaths only, no births or surviving infants, so it cannot supply incidence denominators.
  Period: deaths 2004-2019 in the export (24,314 cases); participation ramps up 2004-2007 (248 to 1,197 cases a year), about 1,250-1,670 a year 2008-2013 and 1,930-2,100 a year 2014-2019; the manuscript uses 2008-2019. Changes in case counts over time reflect participation, not incidence.
  Geography: de-identified: state fields are randomized codes (42 reviewing-state codes; death state blank for 51%); no state names, no county, no urban/rural. The 22 jurisdictions in the codebook header are the CDC SUID Case Registry subset, not all reviewing states.
  Linkage: none: no identifier shared with PRAMS or the CDC files, and randomized state codes prevent even state-level joins.
  Missing answers: documented per item; unknown is a separate answer, never exposed.
- prams_p8_arf (PRAMS Phase 8 Analytic Research File codebook). Role: population reference.
  One record: one sampled mother of a live birth, surveyed a few months after the birth.
  Covers: weighted survey of mothers a few months after a live birth, sampled from birth certificates in participating states; not designed to count infant deaths.
  Period: Phase 8 (the bed-sharing manuscript uses 2016-2021, 43 sites).
  Geography: participating sites only; NCHS urban/rural (2 levels) available; no case source has urban/rural.
  Linkage: none at the individual level: group-level comparisons with case series only.
  Survey weight (required for any prevalence): WTANAL.
  Missing answers: .B = don't know or blank, .S = skipped; never count these as exposed.
- prams_p8_std2 (PRAMS Phase 8 Standard Section II codebook). Role: population reference.
  One record: one sampled mother of a live birth, surveyed a few months after the birth.
  Covers: weighted survey of mothers a few months after a live birth, sampled from birth certificates in participating states; not designed to count infant deaths.
  Period: Phase 8.
  Geography: participating sites only.
  Linkage: none at the individual level: group-level comparisons with case series only; its items are used with the Phase 8 ARF, whose WTANAL weight applies.
  Missing answers: don't know is coded separately (e.g. 7777); never count it as exposed.
- prams_p7_arf (PRAMS Phase 7 Analytic Research File codebook). Role: population reference.
  One record: one sampled mother of a live birth, surveyed a few months after the birth.
  Covers: weighted survey of mothers a few months after a live birth, sampled from birth certificates in participating states; not designed to count infant deaths.
  Period: Phase 7 (2012-2015).
  Geography: participating sites only; NCHS urban/rural (2 levels) available; no case source has urban/rural.
  Linkage: none at the individual level: group-level comparisons with case series only.
  Survey weight (required for any prevalence): WTANAL.
  Missing answers: .B = don't know or blank, .S = skipped; never count these as exposed.

Task: propose exactly 5 distinct research questions that use the design given at the end of this message. They form a pool that is checked and narrowed down later, so aim for range and originality; feasibility, novelty and importance are scored afterwards.
Rules:
- Ask questions a specialist would not think of first. Do not propose a question the manuscripts already answered, or one that only adds another risk factor or effect modifier to the models they fit.
- Respect the source roles: outcomes come only from case series, exposure prevalence only from population reference sources (using their survey weight), and the population at risk only from denominator sources. List each source you use under the role it plays in this question; leave a role empty if the question does not use it.
- `comparison`: who is compared with whom, in which period. Check that the periods of the sources you combine overlap.
- Think outside the field's usual questions. At least 2 ideas must be built mainly on inventory domains marked NEW (no manuscript uses them). The domain matches below show where a case series and a population reference record similar things, including comparisons no manuscript has made.
- `domains`: the inventory domains the question uses, each copied exactly as its label (`source_id / domain name`), from sources you list under a role.
- `question`: one sentence. `why_open`: one or two sentences on why it is unanswered and what an answer would change. `data`: how those domains would be used.
- Do not invent variable names, and do not propose a question that needs data no source documents.

What the manuscripts studied:
## SUID_manuscript_v9_clean
Question: To test whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) reflects a constant effect from birth or a developmentally timed phenomenon by applying a postconceptional age (PCA) alignment framework that accounts for differences in maturity at birth.
Question: To determine the incidence rate ratios of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) across different developmental windows.
- hypothesis: The study tests whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is present from birth or emerges at a specific developmental stage.
- finding: Among the eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
- finding: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak but diverged after the peak with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
- finding: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window (36–42 PCA weeks) but higher male incidence in the late window (≥47 PCA weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking was associated with higher SUID incidence across both windows.
- limitation: The analysis excludes a small number of deaths at the extremes of the PCA distribution, including some extremely and very preterm infants who died early in postnatal life.
- limitation: The models did not account for postnatal exposures that may change during infancy, such as breastfeeding.
- limitation: The study uses vital-record data, which may have exposure and cause-of-death misclassification issues.
- future_work: Future research will focus on understanding the long-term consequences of separation from the mother in human infants and how it may predispose males to increased vulnerability to SIDS.
- future_work: The study suggests that interventions targeting socioeconomic and environmental stressors may represent an important avenue for reducing risk in infants beyond the early peak period.
Variables used: Breastfeeding status at discharge (covariate); Infant sex (exposure); Maternal smoking during pregnancy (covariate); Postconceptional age (PCA) (covariate); Preterm birth (covariate); SUID (outcome); Sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) (outcome); maternal smoking during pregnancy (exposure); postconceptional age (exposure); preterm birth (stratifier); sex (stratifier); year of birth or death (stratifier)

## bedsharing_ms_v7
Question: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
Question: To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
Question: To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
- hypothesis: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
- finding: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
- finding: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
- finding: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
- finding: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
- finding: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
- finding: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
- finding: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
- finding: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
- finding: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
- limitation: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
- limitation: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
- limitation: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
- limitation: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
- limitation: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
- limitation: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
- limitation: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
- limitation: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
- limitation: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
- limitation: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
- limitation: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.
Variables used: PCA (postconceptional age) (outcome); Sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) (outcome); bed sharing (effect_modifier); bed sharing (exposure); birthweight (low, non-low) (stratifier); birthweight (stratifier); chronological age (offset); maternal smoking during pregnancy (covariate); maternal smoking during pregnancy (effect_modifier); maternal smoking during pregnancy (exposure); maternal smoking status (smoking, non-smoking) (stratifier); postconceptional age (exposure); preterm birth (covariate); preterm birth (effect_modifier); preterm birth (exposure); sex (male, female) (stratifier); sex (stratifier)

## SUID literature from the Ramirez lab and Lavista Ferres group: abstracts (PubMed, retrieved 2026-10-26)
Question: To determine whether maternal obesity is a risk factor for Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) and the proportion of SUID cases attributable to maternal obesity.
Question: To examine pandemic-era changes in non-SUID infant mortality by gestational age, age at death and cause of death.
Question: To investigate the effects of maternal prepregnancy smoking, reduction during pregnancy, and smoking during pregnancy on SUID rates.
Question: To assess whether inner ear dysfunction not only weakens the hypercapnic response, but also plays a role in suppressing the arousal response to suffocating gas mixtures.
Question: To investigate the role of PiCo and preBötC in respiratory-sympathetic coupling under control conditions and following exposure to chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH).
Question: To report results from an 11-step user-centered design development process for a quit smoking conversational chatbot called QuitBot.
Question: To investigate whether mouse models of Leigh Syndrome exhibit dysfunctions in neuromuscular activity of swallow and breathing integration.
Question: How does chronic intermittent hypoxia (IH) affect adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus?
Question: What are the effects of IH on synaptic plasticity in the dentate gyrus?
Question: Do reactive oxygen species (ROS)-dependent and ROS-independent mechanisms contribute to changes in adult neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity due to IH?
Question: How do breathing patterns during the first hour after birth predict survival in mice born prematurely or at term?
Question: What are the roles of inhibition within the pre-Bötzinger complex (preBötC) for rhythm generation?
Question: Does chronic intermittent hypoxia differentially impact inspiratory activity states at the level of the preBötzinger Complex?
Question: Can progesterone pretreatment ameliorate detrimental effects of lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation on cortical neurogenesis in mice?
- finding: The overall non-SUID infant mortality rates consistently trended downwards with no pandemic-associated change.
- finding: Mortality rates among full-term infants reversed their prepandemic declines during the pandemic.
- finding: Postneonatal deaths also reversed their prepandemic decline with statistically significant increases during the pandemic.
- finding: The decline in early neonatal mortality rates became more pronounced during the pandemic.
- finding: Rates of mortality due to external causes increased during the pandemic.
- finding: Variants in 88 genes were identified, with 64.6% of infants having variants of interest.
- finding: Seventy-three of the identified gene variants have been previously associated with SIDS/SUID/SUDP.
- finding: Forty-three cardiac genes were identified, related to cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, and other conditions.
- finding: Eight gene variants are implicated in the response to hypoxia and regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
- finding: Maternal obesity is a risk factor for Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID), with an increased risk associated with higher maternal BMI.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy significantly increases the risk of SUID.
- finding: Post-hypoxic recovery of respiration is gender dependent, which is centrally manifested at the level of the preBötzinger complex (preBötC).
- finding: Sighs monitor changes in brain states and induce arousal, playing a role in homeostatically regulating breathing stability under physiological and pathological conditions.
- finding: Inner ear dysfunction (IED) can suppress the movement response to hypoxia-hypercarbia in mice, potentially playing a role in Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS).
- finding: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) is critical for generating breathing rhythms, and its function can be influenced by gender.
- finding: A prior study identified an association between hearing suppression on the newborn hearing test and subsequent death from SIDS.
- finding: Inner ear dysfunction precipitates a marked suppression of the hypercapnic ventilatory response (HCVR).
- finding: Inner ear dysfunction weakens the hypercapnic response and suppresses the arousal response to suffocating gas mixtures.
- finding: The HCVR was significantly decreased in bilateral and unilateral IT-Gent-treated mice compared to controls.
- finding: Arousal movements were suppressed in bilateral and unilateral IT-Gent-treated mice compared to controls.
- finding: Inner ear dysfunction could be relevant in the pathophysiology of SIDS.
- finding: Inner ear dysfunction plays a key role in arousal from suffocating gas mixtures.
- finding: Swallow-related submental complex duration and amplitude were significantly decreased in both Mecp2-/y and Mecp2+/- mice compared to wild-type.
- finding: Cholinergic immunoreactivity in the hypoglossal, facial, and trigeminal motor nuclei was decreased in postsymptomatic Mecp2-deficient mice.
- finding: The transition time from inspiration to swallow was significantly increased in Mecp2-/y mice.
- finding: The study investigates the role of PiCo and preBötC in respiratory-sympathetic coupling under control conditions and following exposure to chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH).
- finding: Baseline sympathetic nerve activity increased, breathing frequency increased, and expiratory time decreased following CIH exposure.
- finding: Stimulation of PiCo specific cholinergic-glutamatergic neurons caused a sympathetic burst during all phases of the respiratory cycle in control mice but only during postinspiration and late expiration in CIH mice.
- finding: Stimulation of glutamatergic PiCo neurons increased cervical sympathetic nerve (cSN) activity during the postinspiratory phase in both control and CIH mice.
- finding: Optogenetic stimulation of ChAT containing neurons in the PiCo area did not affect sympathetic activity under either control or CIH conditions.
- finding: Stimulation of Dbx1 or Vglut2 neurons in preBötC evoked an inspiration and a concomitant cSN burst under both control and CIH conditions.
- finding: PiCo and preBötC contribute to respiratory-sympathetic coupling, which is altered by chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH).
- hypothesis: It is hypothesized that adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus maintains normal hippocampal function.
- finding: Chronic intermittent hypoxia did not affect paired-pulse facilitation but suppressed long-term potentiation (LTP).
- finding: Chronic intermittent hypoxia increased the number of proliferating Sox2+ neural progenitor cells but reduced the number of doublecortin-positive neurons.
- finding: Chronic intermittent hypoxia increased radial glial cell proportion and decreased adult-born neuron proportion in the dentate gyrus.
- finding: Antioxidant treatment mitigated chronic intermittent hypoxia-dependent suppression of LTP and prevented loss of adult-born neurons.
- hypothesis: Breathing patterns in the first hour after birth predict survival in premature mice.
- finding: Mortality was significantly increased in premature pups born at gestational day 18.5 after maternal LPS injection.
- finding: Mice that survived had higher birth weights and showed eupneic or gasping activity transitioning into normal breathing.
- finding: Mice that did not survive exhibited distinct large amplitude breaths at low frequency, failing to transition into normal breathing.
- hypothesis: Local inhibition destabilizes rhythmogenesis while long-range inhibition stabilizes it in the pre-Bötzinger complex inspiratory microcircuit.
- finding: Partial excitation block leads to increased rhythmic variability but recovers after blockade of inhibition in the pre-Bötzinger complex.
- hypothesis: Chronic intermittent hypoxia differentially impacts inspiratory activity states at the level of the pre-Bötzinger complex.
- finding: Chronic intermittent hypoxia increased irregularity score (IrS) and fluctuation value (χ) but did not affect sample entropy (sENT) of amplitude in baseline conditions.
- finding: During hypoxia, all slices from CIH-exposed mice exhibited rhythms throughout the interval, while only a fraction of control rhythms maintained rhythmicity.
- hypothesis: Progesterone pretreatment ameliorates detrimental effects of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammation on cortical neurogenesis in mice.
- finding: Lipopolysaccharide exposure reduced Tbr2 intermediate neural progenitor cell density but increased microglia activation and cell death rates.
- finding: Pre-exposure with progesterone statistically increased Tbr2 intermediate neural progenitors and protected against cell death induced by LPS.
- hypothesis: Chronic intermittent hypoxia alters local respiratory circuit function at the level of the pre-Bötzinger complex.
- finding: Chronic intermittent hypoxia increased lipid peroxidation in the pre-Bötzinger complex, which was reduced by antioxidant treatment.
- hypothesis: Excessive sensory stimulation during development alters neural plasticity and vulnerability to cocaine in mice.
- finding: Mice exposed to excessive sensory stimulation showed enhanced reinforcing properties of cocaine but impaired persistence of cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization.
- finding: Excessive sensory stimulation altered glutamatergic transmission in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala, affecting behaviors related to addiction.
- hypothesis: Microcircuits in respiratory rhythm generation share commonalities with other rhythm generating networks, including synaptic inhibition and excitation roles.

What the manuscripts studied:
## SUID_manuscript_v9_clean
Question: To test whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) reflects a constant effect from birth or a developmentally timed phenomenon by applying a postconceptional age (PCA) alignment framework that accounts for differences in maturity at birth.
Question: To determine the incidence rate ratios of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) across different developmental windows.
- hypothesis: The study tests whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is present from birth or emerges at a specific developmental stage.
- finding: Among the eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
- finding: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak but diverged after the peak with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
- finding: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window (36–42 PCA weeks) but higher male incidence in the late window (≥47 PCA weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking was associated with higher SUID incidence across both windows.
- limitation: The analysis excludes a small number of deaths at the extremes of the PCA distribution, including some extremely and very preterm infants who died early in postnatal life.
- limitation: The models did not account for postnatal exposures that may change during infancy, such as breastfeeding.
- limitation: The study uses vital-record data, which may have exposure and cause-of-death misclassification issues.
- future_work: Future research will focus on understanding the long-term consequences of separation from the mother in human infants and how it may predispose males to increased vulnerability to SIDS.
- future_work: The study suggests that interventions targeting socioeconomic and environmental stressors may represent an important avenue for reducing risk in infants beyond the early peak period.
Variables used: Breastfeeding status at discharge (covariate); Infant sex (exposure); Maternal smoking during pregnancy (covariate); Postconceptional age (PCA) (covariate); Preterm birth (covariate); SUID (outcome); Sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) (outcome); maternal smoking during pregnancy (exposure); postconceptional age (exposure); preterm birth (stratifier); sex (stratifier); year of birth or death (stratifier)

## bedsharing_ms_v7
Question: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
Question: To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
Question: To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
- hypothesis: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
- finding: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
- finding: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
- finding: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
- finding: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
- finding: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
- finding: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
- finding: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
- finding: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
- finding: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
- limitation: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
- limitation: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
- limitation: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
- limitation: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
- limitation: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
- limitation: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
- limitation: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
- limitation: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
- limitation: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
- limitation: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
- limitation: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.

What the manuscripts studied:
## SUID_manuscript_v9_clean
Question: To test whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) reflects a constant effect from birth or a developmentally timed phenomenon by applying a postconceptional age (PCA) alignment framework that accounts for differences in maturity at birth.
Question: To determine the incidence rate ratios of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) across different developmental windows.
- hypothesis: The study tests whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is present from birth or emerges at a specific developmental stage.
- finding: Among the eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
- finding: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak but diverged after the peak with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
- finding: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window (36–42 PCA weeks) but higher male incidence in the late window (≥47 PCA weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking was associated with higher SUID incidence across both windows.
- limitation: The analysis excludes a small number of deaths at the extremes of the PCA distribution, including some extremely and very preterm infants who died early in postnatal life.
- limitation: The models did not account for postnatal exposures that may change during infancy, such as breastfeeding.
- limitation: The study uses vital-record data, which may have exposure and cause-of-death misclassification issues.

## bedsharing_ms_v7
Question: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
Question: To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
Question: To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
- hypothesis: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
- finding: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
- finding: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
- finding: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
- finding: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
- finding: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
- finding: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
- finding: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
- finding: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
- finding: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
- limitation: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
- limitation: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
- limitation: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
- limitation: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
- limitation: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
- limitation: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
- limitation: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
- limitation: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
- limitation: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
- limitation: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
- limitation: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.

What the manuscripts studied:
## SUID_manuscript_v9_clean
Question: To test whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) reflects a constant effect from birth or a developmentally timed phenomenon by applying a postconceptional age (PCA) alignment framework that accounts for differences in maturity at birth.
Question: To determine the incidence rate ratios of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) across different developmental windows.
- hypothesis: The study tests whether male excess risk in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is present from birth or emerges at a specific developmental stage.
- finding: Among the eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
- finding: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak but diverged after the peak with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
- finding: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window (36–42 PCA weeks) but higher male incidence in the late window (≥47 PCA weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking was associated with higher SUID incidence across both windows.
- limitation: The analysis excludes a small number of deaths at the extremes of the PCA distribution, including some extremely and very preterm infants who died early in postnatal life.
- limitation: The models did not account for postnatal exposures that may change during infancy, such as breastfeeding.
- limitation: The study uses vital-record data, which may have exposure and cause-of-death misclassification issues.
- future_work: Future research will focus on understanding the long-term consequences of separation from the mother in human infants and how it may predispose males to increased vulnerability to SIDS.
- future_work: The study suggests that interventions targeting socioeconomic and environmental stressors may represent an important avenue for reducing risk in infants beyond the early peak period.

## bedsharing_ms_v7
Question: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
Question: To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
Question: To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
- hypothesis: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
- finding: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
- finding: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
- finding: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
- finding: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
- finding: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
- finding: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
- finding: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
- finding: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
- finding: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
- finding: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
- finding: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
- finding: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
- limitation: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
- limitation: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
- limitation: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
- limitation: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
- limitation: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
- limitation: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
- limitation: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
- limitation: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
- limitation: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
- limitation: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
- limitation: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.
